14.0.s.en: (2) The woman who poured the ointment

14.0.0.en: After St. Mark has dealt with the priests' plot on Wednesday night, he takes us back to the previous Sunday night (Jn 12:1), where the feast was which the Lord Jesus attended in the house of Simon who had been a leper and whom the Lord healed.

14.0.1.en: "Bethany": it means "house of affliction", and it is a village lying at the foot of the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem, and the Lord used to spend the night in it, and to spend the day in Jerusalem throughout the week of the Passion.

14.0.2.en: "There came a woman": Matthew and Mark also do not mention who this woman is, while St. John confirmed that she was Mary, the sister of Lazarus and Martha (Jn 12:3).

14.0.4.en: "Ointment of spikenard": it is the costliest and most fragrant of perfumes in that time, and it was also pure, that is, concentrated. So she broke the box, that is, the neck of the flask, and poured it on Christ's head. And St. John says that she poured it on His feet, which leads us to conclude that she poured the ointment on His head and His feet.

14.1.0.en: Because of Mary's action, many of those present were indignant, some of them from among the disciples (Mt 26:

14.1.1.en: 8), and St. John pointed out that the most indignant of them was Judas (Jn 12:4), and they asked within themselves: why this waste, were not the poor more deserving of its costly price, 300 (denarii)?

14.1.3.en: To know how high the price of this ointment was, the wage of a laborer for a day was one denarius (Mt 20:2), and if we subtract the days of the Sabbaths on which work was not permitted, the price of the flask of ointment was equal to a laborer's wage for a whole year.

14.2.0.en: The people's rebuke and reproach of her increased, so the Lord Christ intervened in her defense, and repelled every attack on her, indeed He reproved those who reproached her and praised her action, making clear: the poor you have with you always, but My days on earth are few ... and He never rejects the feelings of love offered to Him by His children and His beloved.

14.3.0.en: What Mary did was as though a prophecy from her of Christ's crucifixion and burial, and this is what Christ declared, that it was for the burying. And Christ was not content only to thank her or praise her, but commanded His pure Apostles to record this event in their Gospels when writing and preaching, so that the whole world might know what Mary, the sister of Lazarus, did, and call her blessed ... We learn from this event:

14.3.1.en: (1) That Mary offered the dearest thing she had to Christ the Lord ... so what do we offer?

14.3.2.en: (2) This was an offering of thanks to Christ who raised her brother ... do we thank God for His works with us ... and how do we thank Him?

14.3.3.en: (3) Would that we did not condemn anyone for his action ... for the one we condemn may be praised by God Himself. (4) God does not forget the labor of love, and praises and encourages His children and calls them blessed ... how good is His heart.

14.4.0.en: "The first day of unleavened bread": it was Thursday, and on it the leaven was removed from the houses. And the Passover lamb was slaughtered between the third and fifth hours in the afternoon, but it was not eaten before sunset, that is, Friday night, and on that day His disciples asked Him: where shall we go and prepare that Thou mayest eat the Passover?

14.5.0.en: Since Christ did not want to declare the place openly, lest Judas know and report to the priests, and the disciples be exposed to the danger of being arrested, He sent Peter and John, and gave them a sign that they would meet a man bearing a pitcher of water and follow him to the house, then ask the master of the house about the place, and he would show them a place at the top of the house, "a large upper room furnished". And there the two disciples were to prepare the Passover for the Lord and the rest of the disciples. And let us note the following:

14.5.1.en: (1) The Lord Jesus, and none of His disciples, had a house in Jerusalem, and therefore He used another man's house.

14.5.2.en: (2) Church tradition tells us that this house is the house of St. Mark, the preacher of all the land of Egypt.

14.5.3.en: (3) The Lord Jesus used the sign of the "pitcher of water" before the institution of the Eucharist (the sacrament of Communion), in a clear indication that Baptism by water precedes Communion.

14.6.0.en: In the evening (that is, Friday night), the Lord Christ came with His disciples to the place prepared for eating the Passover. And as they sat down to eat, Christ made an announcement that fell like a thunderbolt on His disciples, namely that one of the Twelve would betray Him, and that he was one of those who eat with Him.

14.7.0.en: The disciples' feeling changed from joy in celebrating the most splendid of the Jews' feasts to sorrow and bewilderment, and they began to ask aloud, one after another: "Is it I?" And a confirming answer came: yes, it is one of you. And He gave another sign, that the one who betrays Him would dip his hand in the same dish from which Christ eats. And St. John adds in his Gospel (Jn 13:26) that Jesus indeed dipped the sop in the dish and gave it to Judas to eat, as a final silent indication that Judas was His betrayer ... all these calls, hints and warnings had as their purpose Judas' repentance. But the picture shows us how the evil heart that loves money did not respond to God's warnings, despite their clarity and repetition. In addition to that, we find that Judas attended the Passover with everyone although he was determined to betray Christ, but in obvious hypocrisy he took part in this table ... do we do like him at times?!

14.7.1.en: May the Lord give us a watchful, sensitive heart, quick to respond and to return from the way of evil...

14.8.0.en: The Lord affirmed that He is going on His way for the redemption of mankind as it was in the prophecies, but this does not excuse Judas from the punishment of his treachery and betrayal, for God did not make Judas betray Him, and He could have been arrested and crucified without Judas having any part in it, but Judas by his deed deserved the punishment of his destruction. "It had been good ... if he had never been born": an expression by way of illustration, and it carries a figure of the severity of this man's punishment, so that it would have been better for him not to be born than to be born and fall into this evil and sin, and deserve this terrible judgment.

14.9.s.en: (5) The institution of the Eucharist, "the sacrament of Communion"

14.9.0.en: After the supper of the lamb, the Lord took bread and blessed it, and it changed into His true Body in a transcendent, mystical manner, and He declared quite clearly that this bread had become His Body, "Take, eat: this is My body", and He presented and gave this Body to them to eat ... and therefore the Church has kept in her Divine Liturgy the same words that the Lord Christ uttered.

14.10.0.en: And He did likewise also with the cup, which contained wine mixed with water - as was the custom at the Passover - and He gave thanks also and gave it to the disciples to drink, the cup being passed among them, and the Lord also declared clearly the change of the wine into His true Blood shed for the world for its salvation and redemption.

14.11.0.en: Thus the Lord accepted in Himself the sentence of death by His own will and authority before the Jews carried it out on Him, and declared that He would not repeat this mystery with them again on earth, since He was content with instituting it before His death. But He promised that there would be a new feast and fellowship in the Kingdom of Heaven, where we shall be spirits feeling and being satisfied with Him in a spiritual manner far from material eating, and therefore the expression "drink it new" is a figurative expression whose purpose is what has been explained before.

14.11.1.en: V.: "And when they had sung an hymn": the psalms of praise (Ps 115-118), known to the Jews, were sung after the Passover supper. And when they finished the singing, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

14.12.0.en: In His last talk with His disciples, and before delivering Himself up, the Lord began to prepare them for the battles they were about to face, and He showed them the first of them, which is doubt of Him, as they would see Him delivered into the hands of the Jews without resistance, and in an appearance of weakness. And as a result of this situation, they would flee and be scattered like sheep that have lost their shepherd, and the Lord here used the same meaning that Zechariah uttered in (Zech 13:7).

14.13.0.en: The Lord did not leave them long in this state - of anxiety and disturbance - but declared with assurance that He would rise from the dead, and would meet them in Galilee. And of course, not all Christ's words were understood by them, but they came to be sure of them after they happened.

14.14.0.en: As was Peter's custom, being always the first to speak or object, and with a mistaken feeling about himself that he was better than the rest of the disciples, he declared, with an impulsive, unconsidered emotion, that he was the only one who would not doubt and would not leave Christ, even if he remained alone and the rest of the disciples left Him.

14.15.0.en: In response to Peter's pride and conceit, Christ confronted him with what he would do and perform, for he alone, apart from all the disciples, would deny Him three times during His trial. And the Fathers see, in a symbolic contemplation, that the crowing of the cock twice is a symbol of God's warnings in the two Covenants (the Old and the New), and that Peter's threefold denial is a symbol of the completeness of man's denial of God in his weakness, as he denies Him in thought, word and heart. But Peter repeated and insisted on what he had said before, and so said all of them also, that is, the rest of the disciples, in affirming that they had no doubt and wished to die with Christ.

14.15.1.en: My friend ... trust in God and in oneself in Christ is good, so long as self does not enter into it ... therefore, always ask God's help in humility, and He will support your human weakness, and strengthen you and give you victory in the hard time.

14.15.4.en: 32- And they came to a place which was named Gethsemane: and He saith to His disciples, "Sit ye here, while I shall pray."

14.15.5.en: 33- And He taketh with Him Peter and James and John, and began to be sore amazed, and to be very heavy; 34- And saith unto them, "My soul is exceeding sorrowful unto death: tarry ye here, and watch." 35- And He went forward a little, and fell on the ground, and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from Him. 36- And He said, "Abba, Father, all things are possible unto Thee; take away this cup from Me: nevertheless not what I will, but what Thou wilt." 37- And He cometh, and findeth them sleeping, and saith unto Peter, "Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour? 38- Watch ye and pray, lest ye enter into temptation. The spirit truly is ready, but the flesh is weak." 39- And again He went away, and prayed, and spake the same words. 40- And when He returned, He found them asleep again, (for their eyes were heavy,) neither wist they what to answer Him. 41- And He cometh the third time, and saith unto them, "Sleep on now, and take your rest: it is enough, the hour is come; behold, the Son of man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. 42- Rise up, let us go; lo, he that betrayeth Me is at hand." 43- And immediately, while He yet spake, cometh Judas, one of the twelve, and with him a great multitude with swords and staves, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. 44- And he that betrayed Him had given them a token, saying, "Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is He; take Him, and lead Him away safely." 45- And as soon as he was come, he goeth straightway to Him, and saith, "Master, master;" and kissed Him. 46- And they laid their hands on Him, and took Him. 47- And one of them that stood by drew a sword, and smote a servant of the high priest, and cut off his ear.

14.15.6.en: 48- And Jesus answered and said unto them, "Are ye come out, as against a thief, with swords and with staves to take Me? 49- I was daily with you in the temple teaching, and ye took Me not: but the scriptures must be fulfilled." 50- And they all forsook Him, and fled.

14.15.7.en: 51- And there followed Him a certain young man, having a linen cloth cast about his naked body; and the young men laid hold on him: 52- And he left the linen cloth, and fled from them naked.

14.16.0.en: On a part of the Mount of Olives, there was the garden of Gethsemane, which means "oil press", because of the many olive trees in it.

14.16.1.en: The Lord commanded the Twelve to sit, then chose from them three, Peter, James and John, who had seen Him in the glory of the transfiguration, so that they would not stumble when they saw Him in suffering and weakness during His prayer and His last hours before His arrest, trial and crucifixion. And indeed, they saw His face with the signs of human pain and distress showing on it.

14.17.0.en: The Lord Jesus did not hide His human feelings from His disciples, but was frank with them about them, saying:

14.17.1.en: "My soul is exceeding sorrowful unto death", that is, the sorrow reached its utmost within Him, for He knows in His divinity what is coming upon Him. And His human sorrow was a compound sorrow, if the expression is permissible, because:

14.17.2.en: (1) Christ sorrowed because, being innocent and pure, He began to bear all the sins of the evil world, and what a weight and burden, as He bears all the evil and uncleanness.

14.17.3.en: (2) Christ also sorrowed because - as a man - injustice would fall upon Him, since redemption requires the death of an innocent one without sin on behalf of a sinful mankind.

14.17.4.en: And therefore, despite His submitting by His own will to what was coming upon Him and what He knew, He prayed to the Father in His humanity asking that these sufferings be taken from Him, in proof of His perfect humanity.

14.18.0.en: "Abba, Father": an expression transferred from the Chaldean language to the Aramaic dialect, and it was known among the Jews. St. Paul also used it in (Rom; 8:15, Gal 4:6). The two words carry one meaning, namely "Father", but as one expression they carry deeper meanings of love, familiarity and strong attachment, and to understand it well, we compare it to the colloquial expression "Yaba, ya abouya" (Daddy, my father).

14.18.1.en: We are still in the same scene with all its bitter feelings and sufferings, as the Lord Jesus lifts His heart to the heavenly Father who is able to do all things, asking Him to take from Him the sufferings of the cross. But He - in perfect obedience - surrenders His will to the Father, declaring His submission to accept it.

14.18.2.en: Would that we learned from this scene the acceptance of God's will in our lives, and learned from our Savior the persistence of prayer as He did, and did not hide our feelings from God however sad or bitter they may be, and let us trust that as long as He has allowed them, He will help us in them and against them...

14.19.0.en: Christ had gone a little further from His disciples to be alone with the Father in His prayer, and on His return He found the disciples sleeping, and He addressed Peter reproachfully: "Couldest not thou watch with Me in My sufferings even one hour?" But the gentle and kind Christ, after His reproach, made an excuse for Peter and the two disciples, that their spiritual will wanted to watch and to complete every spiritual work with Him, but the flesh, with its heaviness and weak will, is often a burden on the spirit and hinders its longing.

14.19.1.en: Yes, my God, for we often claim that our spirits are ready and we give great promises, but the lack of striving makes us carry out none of them ... so let us compel ourselves, even with little striving, and not surrender to the weakness of the flesh, lest we enter into temptation.

14.20.0.en: The Lord went to pray again alone with the same feelings of weakness as before, and returned to His disciples again. And because of the heaviness of their bodies and their drowsiness, He found them asleep again, and they could not answer Him - out of shame - since He had said to them before: "Watch and pray".

14.21.0.en: The Lord Jesus returned a third time to His disciples, and this time He reproached them also with His saying: sleep on ... and take your rest, for the time of the striving of prayer has passed, and the hour of the Son of Man has come, in which He is delivered - by His own will - into the hands of sinners and wicked unjust men.

14.22.0.en: "Rise up, let us go": Christ knew in His divinity the coming of Judas and those with him to arrest Him, so He went Himself to meet them and did not wait to be arrested, for by going, Christ wanted to prove to His disciples and to us that it was He who gave Himself up, and He who knows His hour when it will be.

14.23.0.en: During this talk, which was the last before His arrest, Judas came (knowing the place) and with him a great multitude of servants and men of the chief priests, scribes and elders, each carrying a sword or a thick staff, expecting a struggle with the disciples before arresting the Lord.

14.23.1.en: "Judas, one of the twelve": both St. Matthew and St. Mark used this expression to indicate the hideousness of the betrayal whose source was one of those closest to the Lord Christ throughout the years of His preaching, and what a betrayal!!!

14.24.0.en: The betrayer - Judas - used a sign by which the crowd would know the person of the Lord Jesus, and by a strange irony he used the kiss, which is a sign of love and the greatest friendship, in delivering up the Lord. And in flagrant hypocrisy also, he called Him twice: "Master, master", which is a call of respect and submission from a disciple to his teacher, by which he hides his evil and betrayal. And the words: "lead Him away safely", by them Judas meant that the crowd with him should not make a commotion that would draw attention, and hinder and spoil the operation of arresting Christ.

14.25.0.en: When Judas kissed the Lord, the crowd rushed upon the peaceful Lord. And in sad wonder, St. Augustine describes the scene, saying: "They seized the One who came to set them free!!"

14.25.1.en: There were two swords with the Apostles (Lk 22:38), and what is meant by the sword here is a knife no longer than 30 cm which was used for cutting bread, and one of the two swords was with Peter (Jn 18:10), who was appalled by what he saw, so he hurried and struck the servant of the high priest, and cut off his ear. And the cutting off of the ear here is a symbolic reference to the Jewish nation, which cut off its ears from listening to the Lord.

14.26.0.en: The Lord Christ rebuked and reproached those who came to arrest Him, for this night-time throng looked like an ambush for one of the dangerous thieves, despite His constant presence and appearance all day before the people, and this rebuke is a reference to their real cowardice before Christ, and before the people's attachment to Him, so they resorted to this method. And the Lord also makes clear that what they did is what the prophets prophesied (Ps; 22, Isa; 53, Zech 13:7).

14.27.0.en: "They all forsook Him": what is meant here is the disciples, who, from the shock of the surprise, were afraid in their human weakness and left Christ alone, so that what Christ prophesied in (Jn 16:32) might be fulfilled, that a time would come when the disciples would leave Him alone.

14.28.0.en: "And there followed Him a certain young man": he is St. Mark himself, the writer of the Gospel, and he did not mention his name out of his humility.

14.28.1.en: "A linen cloth": that is, the outer garment. And when some of the young men laid hold on him to arrest him, he was afraid and fled in his underclothes - that is, naked - since he was a young, weak, frightened youth, and he has his excuse in all this, since the disciples themselves fled.

14.29.0.en: The crowd went with the Lord Jesus to the house of the high priest "Caiaphas", where all the chief priests, scribes and Pharisees had gathered in his house. And it is noticed that St. Mark did not mention the going first to the house of "Annas" as it is mentioned in (Jn 18:13), who was the former high priest and father-in-law of "Caiaphas", and was content with the trial that took place in the house of "Caiaphas", who was the current and official high priest at that time. And of the Twelve none went to the house of "Caiaphas" except John, and Peter, who followed him cautiously from afar, and remained outside with the servants warming himself by the fire because of the severe cold (Jn 18:18).

14.30.0.en: "To put Him to death": this word is considered the pivot for explaining these two verses, for the trial was a sham, and the sentence had already been decided by the chief priests and elders, that Christ must be killed. And in order to complete this theatrical scene, they called many to bear witness against Christ with testimonies that would justify their killing Him; and because all the testimonies were false, they differed more than they agreed, and they found nothing against Him.

14.31.0.en: Others bore witness - falsely - that Christ said He would destroy the temple of Solomon and build it in three days, and even in this they differed and did not agree, for what Christ truly said was: destroy this temple, meaning His body and His death (Jn 2:19), and I will raise it up - by Myself - that is, the resurrection of His body also after death on the third day, and therefore their testimonies conflicted.

14.32.0.en: The council reached nothing that agreed with their wish, so "Caiaphas", the president of the council, arose and asked the Lord: do You not defend Yourself against what these people accuse You of? But Christ answered nothing and remained silent as Isaiah prophesied: "He openeth not His mouth: He is brought as a lamb to the slaughter" (Isa 53:7). And when "Caiaphas" lost patience, he asked Christ a direct question: "Art Thou the Christ, the Son of the Blessed (God)?"

14.33.0.en: Christ was silent and did not defend Himself, when the questions and testimonies were false, in order to bear the injustice of the wicked. But when the question was connected with His person and His self, He did not deny Himself, but declared clearly and powerfully that He is the Christ, the Son of the living God, indeed He declared His coming glory that would be revealed in His resurrection and ascension and sitting at the right hand of Power (the Father), and also His fearful second coming on the clouds (Acts 1:11) at the end of the world.

14.34.0.en: Christ's reply to the high priest fell like a thunderbolt - when He declared His divinity and His coming on the clouds - and therefore he cried out in anger declaring: (a) the blasphemy of Christ. (b) that he had no need of witnesses. And his expression of his anger came in an act the Law forbids, namely the rending of his clothes (Lev 10:6, 21:10). And by this act, without his knowing it, the rending of his clothes was a sign of the end of the priesthood of the Old Testament and the nullity of animal sacrifice, and the beginning of the living, continuing law of the New Testament in the person of Christ, who in turn hands over the priesthood to the new Church in the person of the Fathers the Apostles, then the bishops and priests.

14.35.0.en: After this "Caiaphas" asked for the council's opinion, and they agreed with his opinion, and so sentenced Christ to death; and their sentence was not enforceable unless the Roman authority ratified it. As for the assembled Jews and servants, they began to mock Christ in insolence and contempt of His person, until they covered His holy face and struck Him, asking Him: prophesy, and tell us who it is that struck You...

14.35.1.en: My beloved God ... did my sin cost You all these sufferings and insults?! It should have been I who was in Your place ... but You took the form of a servant, and for my sake, my Lord, You did not turn Your face from the shame of spitting (from the Liturgy of St. Gregory).

14.35.2.en: So repent, my soul, and do not despise Him who bore all these sufferings out of love for you...

14.36.0.en: Peter was in the palace beneath, that is, in the courtyard of the palace, where the servants had kindled a fire to warm themselves, and with the light of the fire that made the features of his face clear, one of the maids of the high priest recognized him as one of Christ's disciples, and declared it, saying to him: "And thou also wast with Jesus of Nazareth".

14.37.0.en: To escape the critical situation, Peter went out of the house into the outer passage, after he had denied what the maid said and disowned it. And as he went out, he was surprised by the maid - according to Mark's saying she is the same maid, while Matthew the Apostle says: "another maid saw him" (Mt 26:71) - and there is no contradiction between the two sayings if the first maid was the one who told the second, and the second was the one who went after him to the porch to declare and repeat what the first had said, that he was one of the Lord's disciples.

14.38.0.en: Peter denied again. And after a short time, those present declared and affirmed what they had heard from the maid, and confronted Peter saying: you are one of his followers, because you are a Galilean and your speech is like the speech of your teacher and the rest of the disciples. And here, Peter added to his denial that he cursed and swore, to affirm to them the opposite of what they accused him of, and to remove from himself the suspicion of knowing the Lord Jesus at all!!

14.38.1.en: I fear, my God, to blame Peter for his action, because I find myself at times repeating what he did, for I do not show You in my deeds but hide You, and I almost deny You in the darkness of my words and actions.

14.39.0.en: The cock crew the second time, as the sign the Lord had set (v. 30). And at this second crowing, Peter's absent conscience awoke, and he remembered what the Lord Christ had said to him, and therefore he wept bitterly, declaring his repentance for the sin of denying the Lord.

14.39.1.en: Beloved ... there is no doubt that Peter erred greatly by denying the Lord ... but also, at the sign, he remembered, and offered sincere repentance from a contrite heart ... and we, in many cases, may err like him, through our haste, in disturbing errors. But do we have this heart quick to respond to God's calls to us to repent, He who always awaits the return of His children ... grant us, Lord, tears of repentance like those Peter brought in his contrition. Chapter fifteen: the trial of Christ, His crucifixion, His burial
